label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.

03.one_line: The four steps on page 5 and the 18:44 stop give a newsroom builder a clear first day, but the cover is a bare title and the editor's signature as a control is never named as the point.

10.one_line: The extra pages earn their place through the researcher's dispute and the reviewer 'not a second identity' lines, which are exactly the record I trust, but the promised pictures and cast cards are missing and several pages are half empty.

the_page: The type is comfortable on a laptop: a heavy sans headline, a serif body, a rust rule and a one-line cast bar on every page, and each page holds one idea. But there are no pictures at all; the places where a picture or card should be show as italic stage directions in brackets, and the boxes (words, how to read the scenes, numbered steps) are the only graphic device. Most pages are a third to a half empty, and the contents page and cover are nearly blank, so the book looks unfinished rather than calm.

best_page.why: Five numbered boxes, one action each, ending with a cost and a pointer to the longer edition: it answers 'would you start tomorrow' with a role (you, one agent) and a stopping rule, and I can act on it in five minutes.

worst_page.why: A contents list of ten lines on an otherwise blank page, with no page numbers, no one-line promise per chapter and the editor's note on what changes at each step missing; it wastes the second page that should pull me in.

changes.quote: (One picture: the editor at a lectern with a play button; behind him, the factory's nine stations.)
changes.change: Draw the picture, or remove the bracketed stage direction from the printed page; the same for the cast cards promised on page 4 and the strips on pages 8 and 9.
changes.why: A reader sees a description of a picture instead of the picture, which reads as a draft and breaks the one-idea-per-page calm.

changes.quote: Round 1 of the editions, read by synthetic readers
changes.change: Keep the review stamp out of the running head of the reader's copy, and fill the cover (a one-line promise, the nine-agent cast as a row of initials, the date) instead of leaving two thirds white.
changes.why: The stamp competes with the title on every page, and the cover is the page that must make me want to start.

changes.quote: I kept the line. The book keeps the argument.
changes.change: Say what the argument was and what the editor's signature decided in it, in one plain sentence, in both editions.
changes.why: My deal-breaker is an editor who only rubber-stamps; the page shows a decision happening but never says what the line was, so I cannot tell a real control from a ritual.

changes.quote: Three accounts of why, all kept and dated
changes.change: Put the three accounts of the 95% in the body, one line each with its date, rather than a footnote in a box.
changes.why: Three conflicting reasons for the same stop is the most trustworthy thing in the edition for a source-minded reader, and it is hidden at the foot of a mostly empty page.

changes.quote: found the data said the opposite
changes.change: Name the claim and the figure the researcher checked, even in a clause.
changes.why: A fact-checker's finding is the demonstration of the method; without the claim it is an assertion, and I do not trust claims without sources.

changes.quote: The factory is assembled / The factory runs / The stop, and your own factory / A book about you doing it
changes.change: Turn the four-line contents into a half-page opener with page numbers and a one-line promise per chapter, or fold it into the cover.
changes.why: A mostly blank page between the cover and the first idea loses the reader's momentum; same fault on page 2 of the ten-page edition.

changes.change: Set 'Where this came from' in one typeface and in plain words, with repository paths moved to the online edition; the mix of serif and monospace in a single paragraph looks broken.
changes.why: Source lines are the book's strongest trust signal, but a list of internal file names does not let a reader trace anything, and the type changes mid-line.

changes.quote: Dramatised. Rests on the talk's register and on each member's own debrief.
changes.change: Fill the page: pair the interview with a two-column strip of what each agent said did not work, or merge pages 9 and 10 into one spread.
changes.why: A short page that holds the failures, the part I trust most, ends with more than half its height empty and feels like a slip.

notes: Margins shift between pages 3 and 4 (the text block moves left and right), which looks like a layout fault on a laptop. The stage names (Dev, Deck, ruv-sgit, Conductor) come across well through the tags such as '(happy, the fast one)'; the voices are the best thing here. As a newsroom builder I would start with the researcher and a reviewer, not the conductor; the editions never say which role to hire first. No religious words found.
